title: Thermochemistry
lede: Heat in, heat out. Why hand warmers get hot and cold packs get cold, how much energy it takes to heat water, and what a food Calorie really measures.

sections.md:
## Heat vs temperature
- **Temperature** measures the **average** kinetic energy of particles: how fast they're moving.
- **Heat** is **energy transferred** because of a temperature difference, always flowing from hot to cold.

A bathtub of warm water holds far more heat energy than a cup of boiling water, even though the cup is hotter. More particles, more total energy.

**Units:** the **joule (J)** is the SI unit. 1 **calorie** = 4.184 J. A **food Calorie** (capital C) is a **kilocalorie** = 1,000 calories = 4,184 J.

## Exothermic vs endothermic
| | Exothermic | Endothermic |
|---|---|---|
| Energy | **released** to surroundings | **absorbed** from surroundings |
| Surroundings feel | warmer | colder |
| ΔH (enthalpy change) | **negative** | **positive** |
| Examples | burning fuel, hand warmers (iron rusting fast), respiration | instant cold packs (ammonium nitrate dissolving), melting ice, photosynthesis |

**Bonds and energy:** **breaking** bonds always **absorbs** energy; **forming** bonds always **releases** it. A reaction is exothermic when the bonds formed release more energy than the bonds broken absorbed.

sections.q: An instant cold pack feels cold because the reaction is…
sections.why: It absorbs heat from your hand.

sections.md:
## Specific heat and q = mcΔT
**Specific heat (c)** is the energy needed to raise **1 gram** of a substance by **1 °C**.

| Substance | c (J/g·°C) |
|---|---|
| water | **4.184** (very high) |
| aluminum | 0.897 |
| iron | 0.449 |
| copper | 0.385 |

**q = m · c · ΔT**
- q = heat energy (J)
- m = mass (g)
- c = specific heat
- ΔT = change in temperature (°C)

Water's high specific heat is why coastal climates are mild, why your body (mostly water) holds a steady temperature, and why engines use water-based coolant.

sections.title: Heat some water
sections.problem: How much energy to heat 500 g of water from 20 °C to 80 °C?
sections.answer: **About 125.5 kJ** (≈ 30 food Calories' worth of energy).

sections.md:
## Phase changes take energy without changing temperature
While ice melts, its temperature stays at **0 °C** even as you add heat. The energy goes into breaking the attractions between molecules, not into speeding them up.

- **Heat of fusion** of water: **334 J/g** (melting)
- **Heat of vaporization** of water: about **2,260 J/g** (boiling)

Boiling 1 gram of water takes over **five times** the energy needed to heat it from 0 °C all the way to 100 °C (418 J). That's why **sweating** cools you so well: each gram that evaporates carries off a lot of heat.

sections.q: Why does temperature stay at 0 °C while ice melts?
options: The added energy breaks attractions between molecules instead of raising temperature

sections.md:
## Combustion: energy from fuel
Burning fuel is a strongly **exothermic** reaction with oxygen. Energy content is measured as **heat of combustion**.

| Fuel | Approx. energy |
|---|---|
| gasoline | ~46 MJ/kg |
| diesel | ~45 MJ/kg |
| fat (food) | ~37 kJ/g (= 9 kcal/g) |
| carbohydrate/protein (food) | ~17 kJ/g (= 4 kcal/g) |

The 4-4-9 numbers from nutrition are heats of combustion: your body "burns" food by cellular respiration, a slow, controlled combustion.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Heat ≠ temperature.**
- **Food Calorie = kilocalorie.** A 200 Calorie snack is 200,000 calories.
- **Exothermic ΔH is negative** (the system loses energy).
- **Breaking bonds never releases energy.** It always takes energy.
- **ΔT is a change**, so it's the same in °C and K.

practice.q: An exothermic reaction has ΔH that is…
Energy to heat 100 g of water by 10 °C? (c = 4.184)
Which has the highest specific heat?
A hand warmer gets hot because iron oxidizing is…
Energy to melt 10 g of ice at 0 °C? (heat of fusion 334 J/g)
Energy to heat 2,000 g of engine coolant (treat as water) from 20 °C to 90 °C, in kJ? (1 decimal)
The same 500 J heats 10 g of copper (c = 0.385) by how many °C? (1 decimal)
practice.why: ΔT = q ÷ (mc) = 500 ÷ (10 × 0.385) = 500 ÷ 3.85 ≈ **129.9 °C**. The same energy would warm 10 g of water by only ~12 °C.

practice.q: Why does sweating cool you so effectively?
options: Evaporating water absorbs a large heat of vaporization from your skin
practice.why: About 2,260 J per gram leaves with the evaporating water.

practice.q: A meal-prep container has 600 kcal. How many kJ is that? (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ; nearest whole)
